utterances.text: I believe that our LO, our liaison officer, for the MUP and the liaison officer for the VJ did get deployment locations on occasion but it was not consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to turn next to page 17 in the English and page 19 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the name at the top of your page should be "Byrnes." Do you have that one?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: What page number would that be for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's page 17 in mine.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Page 17 doesn't reflect ... I can refer to the screen, but I don't have a hard copy here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Byrnes is Shaun Byrnes, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I note for the transcript that earlier I was listed as saying that the meeting was the 15th of September with Sainovic and Loncar. That should be the 18th of December in case that's what I said. And it's page 44, line 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Colonel, Byrnes -- Shaun Byrnes is listed as speaking and the second line says: "VJ battle group; 27 vehicles, nine T-72 tanks, starting to dig in at the crop dusting airfield, 6 kilometres south of Podujevo ... this is a clear and outright violation." Do you recall this discussion?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I do. The words that I transcribed here were directly from Shaun Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And skipping the next two lines, again it's still Byrnes: "This is a violation - Byrnes wants them out right away. Clark will raise immediately." Do you know what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, in this particular time-frame and location we were very fearful of a KLA/VJ exchange that would end up being out of hand for us to handle. As you know, Mr. Shaun Byrnes was KDOM and, US KDOM, and he refers to General Clark and his comment about Clark raise immediately that they needed to de-escalate the situation in Podujevo before it got out of hand. The tension was very high. The troop disposition, the heavy weapons that were there, was not going to be good, we were fearful of major problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page you'll see an entry for 19 December at 2130 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S I think we have to go to page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It says: "Call from Shaun Byrnes, situation critical in Podujevo. Recommend we call Ambassador Miles." And the next one is: "Call to Ambassador Miles." How does this relate to the earlier comments from Byrnes? Does it get even worse than what was noted at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right, KDOM and KVM had been working all day trying to get the de-escalation to occur by meaning pulling back the MUP and pulling back the VJ deployment and that wasn't happening, in fact, it was building. So hence the call to the embassy to get the information to Mr. Milosevic to see if he couldn't turn this off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what happened as a result of the call to Ambassador Miles and efforts to contact Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly right after the meeting, but I do know over time we did get the de-escalation and we did get the VJ and the MUP to reduce their numbers up there and not be so -- not be such a provocative deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by "provocative deployment" in that context?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, it was a proportionality of force, I mean, we had VJ with heavy weapons and tanks and artillery, and the KLA of course had small arms. And the fear was was that they would -- the VJ would annihilate the whole village down there where the KLA was supposedly in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go forward a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Page 19. At the top it says 24 December, 1998, 1245. I don't know if that's ... Okay. And it's page 21 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the English it says: "Podujevo events have unravelled somewhat, VJ units deployed once again to Podujevo and threats were levied against a US KDOM vehicle." Further on in the paragraph: "Ambassador Miles confirmed the report and levied a formal protest with the FRY government." Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So it sounds like between the 19th and the 24th the VJ might have backed off a little bit but they returned?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yeah, there was in general an agreement that some of the MUP would pull back and the VJ would pull back. The VJ pulled back not so much with the heavy vehicles or artilleries as they did with the personnel. But they came back, I don't remember exactly the date, and I have to rely on my notes here that that was the date, but they came back in its original strength, in -- responding to KLA activity in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And further down on that page there's another 24 December entry listing General DZ and an update, a single line in the middle there General Loncar says: "DZ said verifiers threaten being shot by VJ." Do you know what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: This was a tension-filled time. Many of us, including myself who had walked past the Pristina barracks were often threatened by VJ soldiers that were standing guard or post outside the walls there. They didn't want any photographs taken of them mounting up and deploying. It was a very, you know -- you had to walk on the other side of the road. KDOM was intrusive and KVM was intrusive to the extent of taking photographs of the deployment, radioing ahead to other units that they are leaving and which way that they were headed. And we were later informed that through the KVM LO for the VJ that they felt that this was a serious issue for their security by advance notification of their deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did KVM take the position that this was something that you were entitled to do?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well we felt that we were entitled to do it especially when we didn't get advance notice of a deployment which was the agreement which was sporadic at best, but generally, you know, we would have expected to get information from the MUP or the VJ of where they were heading the next day. We at least wanted 24-hour notice on what those deployments were. And because we weren't getting that, we tended to kind of camp outside those areas and then follow where they were headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next we could look at page 22 of the English. It's listed as page number 38 at the top in typewriting, if that helps you find it in your hard copy. And this would be page 25 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll tell you, Colonel, I'm starting kind of in a middle of a meeting that appears to have taken place on Christmas eve, 24 December, 1998, at 1850 -- 1815 hours. Present Sainovic, Loncar, Slana, Gordana, and General Lukic. Gordana was an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on this page 22 in the English in e-court at the top we have S; I take it is Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "We have been cooperative of KDOM and KVM." He regrets that issues about the helicopter and security are rejected and not IAW agreement. Is that in accordance with?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then skipping the next entry: "The result of investigation showed no grenade." What was that about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That was an event where Mr. Walker and I had left our apartment and were walking to work and we were confronted by a drunken policeman who was out of uniform and we had our Albanian security with us, and he was verbally abusive to the Albanian security. The tension escalated there. Mr. Walker and I were trying to, you know, separate all of this. And our security guard saw the drunken policeman have a grenade in his hand and throw it and the security took Mr. Walker and put him in a car and he left the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say he was out of uniform, how did you know this person was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He called himself a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page in B/C/S, still on the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see Mike, as a the speaker, saying I was never talked to. Who was Mike?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And Lukic -- before that it said all persons were talked to, is that in connection with investigating this incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Were you ever talked to or was a statement ever taken from you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir. And that was a point of contention in that the investigation was incomplete because not all parties who witnessed the scene were talked to, including the Albanian security guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next to the last -- or two entries above the bottom of the page, S, Sainovic I assume says: "Mistake - people of your mission have not given a statement. I'm asking you to do that right now." Did any policemen take your statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Walker then talks about this was not a real investigation. There was no follow-up?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Not that I am aware of. There certainly wasn't with me as one of the members there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did it ever come up again with Sainovic about your personal security in this incident not being fully investigated?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It did come up again, but it wasn't in the context of requirement of a full meeting, it was just continually used thereafter as an example of non-cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Go to the next page in English, page 23, and this will be page 27 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two more pages to talk about relating to Podujevo. We see DZ speaking in the big paragraph says: "Last Sunday, I saw Loncar in asked him the purpose of the VJ company leaving the Podujevo airfield. He said it had to conduct training on a training arena, returning on Tuesday." Now, this meeting was on the 24th of December which according to my master calendar would have been a Thursday in 1998. So the previous Sunday would have been the 20th of December. Do you recall this discussion that DZ had with Loncar at this meeting on the 24th of December?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I vaguely recall it. I'm familiar with the discussion but.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And DZ goes on to say: "The area was described as 10 kilometres. It had Podujevo and many villages in the training area. It was not an area the way armies understand training area." Do you remember that point being made?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any discussions with anybody in the VJ about what their training areas were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I personally did not, but that was a mission Ambassador Walker had given DZ to understand what their definition of training area was and that's what DZ was up in Podujevo to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that related to part of KVM's job in terms of monitoring the VJ and their activities?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And this sounds like VJ took the position that Podujevo the town itself was within their training area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For tanks to drive through?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then going on a couple more lines it said -- this is DZ saying : "I told him, Loncar, this what a provocative action. The next day a column of the unit went to the south of Podujevo and fired machine fire toward the village. On the way back a KDOM vehicle was hit by fire. This was a provocative exercise. On Tuesday the exercise didn't cease." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did KVM consider this a violation?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We did. And we did in the context that we refer to as provocative because at the time the KLA, also in the area, had not fired. We had a KVM member in the village down there, spent the night with them to ensure that they showed restraint. And we felt it was provocative because there was an effort to try and get the KLA to fire and return fire. And that was one of the things I remember DZ was upset about, was that this is going to create problems for us if you continue to do that and we can't help you when that happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 28 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, at the bottom of this page you'll see it's L speaking, I assume that's Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to 24 in the English, it continues, Loncar speaking, he says: "I told you I am competent to stop firing but not authorised to withdraw forces from Podujevo." So that's Loncar, the VJ representative to this commission saying he is not authorised to withdraw forces?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who was?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I do not know who was authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said sometimes in these meetings Sainovic would call Belgrade. Do you know who he was talking to?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion of who he was talking to based on all your dealings with him and the context of this KVM agreement?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: My view was he was talking to somebody in Milosevic's inner circle to try and get the word to him on what they were going to need to do to resolve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The next entry is DZ speaking again saying he saw a column of 40 vehicles saying proportional rezoned is needed here. Do you know what that meant, "proportional rezones," or is that a typo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Let me just read the whole paragraph just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Those are DZ's words, sir. I'm not exactly sure what he meant, what's needed there. But I know that he was working hard in that period to get the forces that were there dispersed. So that may have been what he referred -- but it's purely conjecture on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But doesn't this relate to the comment you made before about proportionate or disproportionate?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Force size.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He goes on to say: "Overwhelming force was ..."

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, it relates to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap for the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreter. We are speaking too fast after one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: DZ said there a major breach of cease-fire by the VJ and MUP. The next speaker is S, Sainovic?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Sainovic says: "I asked for intervention of the VJ units in that spot." You recall him saying that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to have you look at an excerpt from another document -- well, let me ask you this question: Were you aware of any concerns on the part of the VJ that they were being directed by civilians instead of army commanders?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any concerns by General Loncar or anybody in the VJ that their units were being controlled or directed by civilians instead of VJ commander?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I was not aware of any of that concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like, at this point in the record, like to direct your attention to the 65 ter number 0928. This was one of the VJ collegiums that I showed Phil Coo when he was here. It's been tendered into evidence subject to any objections from the Defence, which we're waiting to get. But I'm assuming that it will be admitted, and if so in connection with this entry in Colonel Phillips's notebook I would ask you to look at 0928 in the English at pages 13 and 14 where General Dimitrijevic is talking about what he called a so-called pretend or real planned exercise in the vicinity of Podujevo and talking about a concern about ensuring that not even Sainovic or any other Sainovic can solve these problems by lightly deciding to use the units. Now, the last -- I think that was the last one I had for Podujevo. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have many objections. First of all, it seems that Mr. Hannis is bringing this to a close. In my view, I think it would be appropriate for the witness to see the text and have his interpretation. We now have Mr. Hannis offering his comments, prompting the witness by way of certain remarks. On the other hand, any mention of any civilians commanding the army, we don't find that in the documents and he is now invoking certain evidence that the witness is not familiar with. Maybe the Chamber is, but the witness has nothing to do with that and he is supposed to state his opinion. I think this way of conducting the examination-in-chief is inappropriate, and we have more of Mr. Hannis's conclusions than the witness's. He should not be doing so. It should be the witness who is supposed to offer his interpretation of what he took down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be happy to show him the excerpt from 00928. My problem was, I don't think that was on my list of notifications of documents I was going to use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That might dig you a hole a little deeper rather than get you out of one, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know, but I have to tell you about that. And I tried to quote from the document itself, but I'm happy to show it to the witness, I think that does make sense if the Court is willing to give me leave to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My problem is that I don't understand or did not understand from your comments that you were seeking to have the witness comment at all. As I understood it, you were saying please for cross-reference, Chamber take note of a certain document not yet an exhibits but which you hoped would be an exhibit. You were stretching the role of an advocate very far Mr. Hannis, but I don't think you were doing what Mr. Djurdjic was concerned you were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, Your Honour. I had -- if we went back in the transcript you may see I had a hesitation when I started to ask him about that because I think I realised that this wasn't on my list so I couldn't show it to him and I was trying to think how to present it, and I did that sort of by the seat of my pants, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well we might leave your pants where they are and when we come to final submissions, no doubt if it is an exhibit by then, this may feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I move from Podujevo though, one last question, Colonel. We looked at some of your photographs, and I think you told us those related to Podujevo in December?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What date -- I saw a date on one of them was the 27th of December, were they all on the same day or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir. They were somewhere on the 25th when we were up there. We were up there, I think, every day, I can't recall how many days, but nearly every day we had tensions up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So during that sort of whole week proceeding and around the 25th of December?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to go to page 43 in the English, and it's page 54 in the B/C/S. This is listed as a meeting on the 22nd of January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic again anxious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Hannis, can you tell me what the date of the meeting is and the time next time you put up a new document. You did say it's the 22nd of December -- no, January it seems for this one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. 22nd of January, 1999. It says: "CIO Meeting Part 11." Can you tell what the acronym CIO is.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That was chairman in office, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What person did that refer to in this context?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That would have been Mr. Vollebaek the Norwegian chairman in office at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. OSCE?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see an entry for, it looks like, AMB, Ambassador Travik [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He was Mr. Vollebaek's assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. It he says: "A sinister activity is ... MUP using orange vehicles." Do you know what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right. Our KVM had observed some of the MUP, not many, but some of the MUP were using their once blue vehicles now having been painted orange to get access into some of the villages. And I say "get access" whether they were blue or orange, they had access, but it was a way to lessen their threat initially in the area there because KVM vehicles were orange, KVM was considered, and the orange vehicles, were considered friendly and safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And more likely to receive easy entry than a blue vehicle that might be MUP?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right. Not likely to be fired upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is about a week after Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page, it's 44 in the English. And page 54 at the bottom in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Says: "Tough week, 2 of our verifiers shot last week." Do you recall what that was about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right, that was two verifiers that as I recall were shot by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then this event has been a setback, Racak?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "The scene in the village of Racak was the most horrifying thing one can imagine." Who wrote this? Is this you speaking?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Those are my notes to myself. I believe I usually kind of wrote those things end of the day in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "A true tragedy, we counted 45 bodies, all were shot in the head?" Next paragraph: "The majority of those killed were older men in their 50s and 60s. We also came across three women and one 12-year-old boy." You were out there on what date.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We were out there between 6.30 and 7.00 in the morning on 16 January.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did you have at that time information or get information about how that operation had proceeded in Racak, who was involved?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Gilbertson who was at one time, I believe, a member of the KDOM, and I'm not sure when, but he was absorbed into our mission as a true verifier - just want to emphasise, was not dual hatted, not KDOM and KVM, but did come to KVM - and he notified the head of missions office that there had been this tragic event at Racak. I believe General Maisonneuve, who I believe was at Prizren region, was also involved in on the scene and was notified of this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you know or what did you learn about what forces had been involved in the action at Racak?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We -- you know, this event, from what I can remember, really began to build around the 8th and 9th of January. There was a couple of MUP policemen that had been killed. And there was a gradual build-up of VJ forces and an increase in the MUP forces. The VJ not so much in and around Stimlje or the Racak area but up on a bluff that overlooked the region. And the MUP were more heavily deployed in Racak and Stimlje proper, setting up check-points and going through the village in good numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the action in which these 45 were killed, who was involved?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The MUP were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any VJ involvement in the incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: The VJ involvement consisted of the shelling into -- into the homes in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before, during, or after the MUP going in?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That was before the MUP went in. The villages typically, in all of these incidents, the village was typically shelled, softened up, then these combat MUP spread throughout the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- when you were out there that morning did you see any VJ presence throughout the area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Saw them at check-points with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And see any VJ equipment, vehicles, whatever in the immediate area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: At the check-points. They were parked there with the MUP vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the hills around the area?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We could see that there was vehicles up there, couldn't ID exactly what they were, but we knew that it was a VJ deployment location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you down near the bottom the page, you have a question: "What do we do next?" And can you read what you wrote there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I made a question: "What do we do next?" I say: "We will continue our mission, continue to verify until it simply becomes too risky and dangerous to carry out our mandate. Remember, we are all unarmed here, very tough situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what you wrote on the 22nd of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what you tried to do?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: That's what we tried to do. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions for the witness. I would like to tender this Exhibit 0564 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01312 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he is not going to talk about the notes, I suppose we can go back into open session now. As long as he is not talking about the notes of interview or the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was waiting for Mr. Djurdjic to indicate where he wanted to start. Do we need to be in private for your commencement, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I would need to organise myself a bit, but we can go back into open session. I think it's still a bit too early for the break, so we can resume in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Open.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can I address you as colonel first of all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, Defence team member of the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic. With me is another Defence team member, Ms. Marie O'Leary. I wanted to share with you that I read all of your statements and notes made as well as the transcript of your testimony in the Milutinovic case, as well as followed what you said today. I will try to put only those questions which have not been put to you until now. Since we are in open session, I would like to start with your engagement with the verification mission. You spoke about that today. I would like to know the following: Prior to the mission itself, had you ever participated in another verification mission or a mission that would be similar to this one in nature?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I made a note here that you said today that you were invited by General Ralston, he made an offer. Can you tell us why you were recommended, what previous activities of yours made you a good candidate for Mr. -- for General Ralston and to be a team member for Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Sir, I was -- I honestly don't know why General Ralston selected me, although I was grateful for the opportunity. Ambassador Walker was the one who asked for me when General Ralston asked, Is there anything that you need to assist you? And Mr. Walker called for me. General Ralston really facilitated making that happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Mr. Walker from an earlier time?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever work together with him?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At that time, was Mr. Walker a State Department employee?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: He was a State Department employee, but he was working at National Defence University as the vice-president. And I was working at National Defence University as an aide-de-camp to the president of the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was one other thing I wanted to ask you. I know from this trial that American generals, in addition to their military backgrounds, have civilian specialties. What was your civilian specialty at university?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't understand the question exactly, but I think you are asking me what did I study at the university? In my undergraduate work I was studying economics and geography.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was offered to you when you were asked to work together with Mr. Walker and his team? What made you accept the offer?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I think whenever you are wearing a uniform and you have trained for years to work in environments like this, it's an excellent opportunity to learn. So I was excited to accept, to be involved in something that I had never been involved in before, but had great interest in international missions. So I accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you apply for a KVM post or were you appointed or sent there, rather, by the US government?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I never applied for the job. I had no idea that I was being looked at for the job. I accepted the job on a Thursday and had a plane ticket on Friday to meet Ambassador Walker in New York. It happened that fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Did you ever conclude a contract, and agreement, with the OSCE Secretariat concerning your engagement with the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by did I "conclude a contract." When I was seconded to work for Ambassador Walker, I was still an active-duty military air force officer sent on what we call temporary duty, initially the duration was not to exceed 30 days, but upon 30 days, I was asked if I would stay longer and I agreed. But I never recall signing any contract that made me an employee of the OSCE. I was always told that I was seconded by the OSCE with the US support to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude based on your answer that, speaking in broad terms, you remained a US official throughout your stay in Pristina between the 4th of November, 1999, and until you left the country on the 20th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I guess a troubling word there for me there is "official." I was an OSCE verifier, I considered myself a verifier, I never wore my military uniform during that whole deployment period. I did not report back to US government officials, I reported through OSCE channels. So I would tell you that I considered myself a true OSCE verifier although I remained an active-duty military officer with the US government.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That is why I raised this issue. Were you an employee of an international organisation, which in this case is the OSCE, or were you an employee of the Government of the United States assigned to assist Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd have to answer that question both as yes. Yes, I was an OSCE employee; yes, I was a US Air Force officer seconded to the OSCE to perform an international mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude then that you continued receiving your salary from the US Air Force during your stay in Kosovo and Metohija as a member of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I received my base pay as an air force officer, and I received per diem from the OSCE for the deployment location.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please expand this further. Which part of your expenses was borne by the Vienna Secretariat, your expenses, while you were in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but which expenses specifically?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: My per diem expenses for food and rent and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me what was your function in the Kosovo Verification Mission headquarters in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: My original position was to arrive as Ambassador Walker's Chief of Staff and his special advisor. My Chief of Staff functions in the early part of the mission consisted of helping locate a facility to stand up the OSCE. It entailed the planning for standing up the mission, getting -- bringing in verifiers. Standing up a training facility. Getting computer networks and phones and all the basic logistics established. Establishing an organisational chart on how the mission would be organised. Later on my duties transferred into the area of being more operational in orientation in the sense that once we got the mission stood up, we began to go to the field more often and observe activities with the verifiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First I'd like you to tell us who appointed you to the position of Chef de Cabinet and in what way, when Mr. Hannis led you in his examination-in-chief, you confirmed that you were the Chef de Cabinet, and now you said so yourself, who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker gave me that title.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Before we left the United States in New York, he defined that that would be my role for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was the Secretariat of the OSCE in Vienna informed thereof that you were appointed as Chief of Staff to Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I would have to assume that they were. I was never myself officially notified that they knew, but when I went and visited Vienna, talk to member states, they knew me as his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The simplest way to establish to determine what somebody's position is is to look at the payroll. Now, did you ever have occasion to see the payroll list, whether it actually identified your position there? For instance, Mr. Michael Phillips, and then your position, what was it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I never saw that payroll.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I'm putting all these questions is that I noticed from what you said, but I think I also observed this in the transcript, that you were an advisor for military matters to Mr. Walker; and today we've heard here twice already that you were the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right. My opening comment was, to you, that I was his Chief of Staff and also his advisor. I was referred as a military advisor, but my role, as I said, we moved into the operational scene, consisted of writing speeches for him, to transcribing notes with him, prepping him for interviews with the press, to visiting military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, sir, when you heard that you were going to deploy on a mission in Kosovo and Metohija, did you undergo any type of preparation for this mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: You mean, medical preparation, or operational preparation, training? What do you refer to exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, you are a pilot, an air force pilot, so I'm not referring to medical preparation, but operational, in the operational sense. Whether you were apprised of where you were going, what the situation was there, what type of situation you can find there? So did you undergo any type of training? And I mean more in political terms than historical.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Right. I had not received any preparation for the area, and I must tell you when I was in Hawaii, I was looking -- I was looking east, I was not looking at Europe, and I had to look up where Kosovo was. And I would also add that my occupation in the air force is not that of a combat pilot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, now I'd like to continue putting questions along this line but I won't. Now, tell me, did you have any idea, did you have any picture in your mind as to what was going on in Yugoslavia, what it was that was happening there? In other words, before you were offered this post by Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not. I was truly caught by surprise to be in the pacific to go to Europe. That wasn't my focus. I had not read a great deal on what was happening there. I was aware of Bosnia, but not of what was happening in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Bosnia now. As far as I understood, you had no business or no missions in operational sense in Bosnia in the 1990s; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion at all to read through some documents that you would be encountering during your verification mission in Kosovo and Metohija, and if so, who provided those documents and which documents were they?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I had no documents to read when we arrived. The deployment came very fast, and I was more concerned of taking care of my family upon my quick departure and getting my personal issues squared away. So there was no documents to travel with, no documents to read. My entry into Kosovo really started in Warsaw, Poland, when we met then the Polish chairman in office who acquainted us with the mission prior to entry of 4 of November into Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this was in early November, the time when you were in Warsaw. Could you tell us what Mr. Geremek told you then in terms of what it was that he expected of you, not necessarily what it was that he expected of Mr. Walker's mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I was a note-taker in that meeting. He did not address me specifically. I was introduced to him as Mr. Walker's assistant and he welcomed me. Mentioned that this should be an exciting opportunity and wished me luck. That was about the extent of my in-briefing to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you ended up in Pristina on the 4th of November. Now, tell us, please, when you arrived there, did you read any documents that you were to comply with or implement during your verification mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I believe I got ahold of what's referred to often as the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement somewhere in the first couple of weeks of our arrival. The first couple of weeks I will tell you were spent more logistically internal to OSCE requirements than they were of political requirements. I don't recall exactly, but I would tell you the first discussion we had on the agreement was in early December with Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Walker trying to lay out a broad understanding of really what the agreement said and what the intent of the agreement would be for us to live up to as an OSCE international mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement was, and how and where did you see it? What form did you see it in?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I saw it in a paper copy. And my interpretation of it was, was a mandate that essentially was to help us arrive at a peaceful solution for some sort of a co-existence between the Serbian and Albanian people in Kosovo, and cease-fire maintenance, until a political solution process could run its course. I do not have the actual agreement in front of me. I could refer to it if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me where you saw this document and who it was who showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I saw it for the first time in Pristina, and I can't recall who showed it to me. I think it might -- I don't think anybody specifically showed it to me. It was just kind of in a stack of papers on my desk that I -- that I had gotten ahold of. I don't recall specifically how I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me then something about the substance of that document. Who signed it, did you see the signatures on the document, and what it was about?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: In general I think the document listed how many verifiers were to come into the mission. I think 2.000 was the number. I don't recall the signatures on the document. Although it was called the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, I don't recall ever seeing Mr. Milosevic's signature on the document. I can't recall specifically the content of the document, haven't looked at it in over ten years, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me then, did you see Mr. Holbrooke's signature on it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall his signature, sir. Not that it wasn't there, I just don't remember if it was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you do with this document when you left Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall what I did with it. It might be part of my own archives somewhere. I don't know what I did with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a personal archive, your own personal files, or did you have an official file as the personal assistant to Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Just some personal files. I never turned any of those files over to any government official or State Department or Department of Defence. Those were, I considered them kind of academic papers, experience papers, that I hope to write about one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I am not going to ask you about your private files, nor do you need to speak about that. All I'm interested in is the official files and archives that you had to keep as the Chief of Staff. What I would like to know is, first of all, whether such files existed at all?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I kept papers that Mr. Walker wanted to maintain. I would consider those official papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me whether these were the official documents of the Kosovo Verification Mission, or?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: They would have been documents of the Kosovo Verification Mission, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you hand over those documents to the OSCE Secretariat in Vienna when you left the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why not?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Because we shredded them when we evacuated our mission, except for just a handful of documents which were really KVM reports that the OSCE in Vienna had anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, we've heard the testimony of Mr. DZ who told us that the entire archive of the OSCE was taken out during the -- or withdrawal of the OSCE Verification Mission, that it was taken to Macedonia when they left. Did Mr. Walker treat the documents, the files, in a different manner than they were treated or held in the OSCE KVM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can tell you the papers that I collected, I shredded, Mr. Walker had papers. Some documents he gave to me, very casual matter to keep on file, but the papers that I collected consisted of everything from press statements, newspaper articles, KDOM reports, some Blue Book reports, some KVM reports. It was not necessary for me to take all of those out because they were already in Vienna. So -- and because we were only allowed to take a certain amount out with us pound-wise, weight-wise, in the evacuation, I shredded a lot of that material. It wasn't shred to keep from anyone, it was shredded just to reduce the load. We didn't -- obviously didn't want to leave them all behind. I would add that I cannot speak to General DZ. I'm quite certain that he would have responsibly taken many of his operational papers with him. But I can't speak to what he did with his archives. And I guess I would be careful to call - and I use this term archives, I realise that - but I would be careful to call my desk drawer an archive. It was just some papers that we had collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, this reminds me, General DZ actually delivered these documents at the Whitehall, and as far as I can see what did you with your files is you handed them over to the State Department; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I never said that I handed anything over to the State Department. The documents that I had were shredded. Reports, I didn't take with me because, as I say, Vienna already had those on file.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, the notes that were shown to us by Mr. Hannis, what did you do with those notes? Where did you file them when you left the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: When we left the KVM, I had my personal notes and I turned those over to the ICTY upon request along with photos in Macedonia and those notes first were allowed to be transcribed for me. And I do believe Helena who was Ambassador Walker's secretary who did work for the State Department actually typed those notes out and gave me the copy because I turned the originals over to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Then it was my misunderstanding. Because I read this to mean that your notes were turned over to the OTP by the US, but you told us that this is how it transpired. Now, when was this happening? Was this in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this would have been 1999. I want to clarify: When we left Kosovo and went to Macedonia, I was interviewed a number of times by the ICTY --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to know about the notes. But obviously it was my erroneous conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time then?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, I've already gone over the time. Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was waiting for some logical break in your line of questioning. We will have our second break now and resume at 5 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, I would like to propose something, and I've already discussed this with Mr. Hannis, but we have addressed this to the Trial Chamber. What I'm talking about is the exhibits that were admitted into evidence in the Milutinovic case relating to the notes prepared by this witness that were put forth to him individually and then admitted into evidence in this case. So my proposal is, and Mr. Hannis has agreed to it, that the list of documents that I provided to the Trial Chamber be admitted into evidence in total so that we don't have to waste any time here by putting them to the witness one by one. So this is my proposal to both Mr. Hannis if he agrees and of course to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection to that. Those exhibits on the list though that are excerpts from his notebooks, I request be entered under seal, and I think there are I think two or four on his list which are not from Phillips' notebooks, I have no problem with them being in the open. But all of those in the notebooks under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the Court Officer in a position to know which is which at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Djurdjic and Mr. Hannis, the proposal you make is a sensible one, but you will need to provide the Court Officer with a list of the exhibits identifying which are to be under seal so that we get it right. Please carry on, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, when you took up position at the verification mission in Kosovo, I understand that it was in the very earliest days of the mission. Could you tell me how the headquarters of the KVM in Pristina were set up. I'm not interested in the regional centres, but just the headquarters, how was it set up and did you participate in its setting up?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, the Norwegians had the responsibility to bring in the computer network to network all of our systems together. We established, I believe, five sections in the organisation underneath the head of mission. I don't recall them all, but one was a political office, and one was an operations office, one was a press office. One was kind of a mission support or logistics office. Human rights office. Each component had a job description that was written for its responsibilities. We were hiring and interviewing both national and international staff to work in the mission. I did some of the hiring for the national staff in the press room, the security guards, drivers, things like that. So it was a period of time that was just, you know, building the necessary logistical requirements to sustain the mission. There was a transportation office, that sort of thing. My role was helping Ambassador Walker build a functional organisational chart that would make his work most efficient. He had asked me on several occasions to cut layers of bureaucracy, so he could be in the field and not be in the office that much. He wanted to be out and about Kosovo. So I looked for ways to organisation a mission that way that would enable him to do that. I would say that my role in doing that, really establishing job descriptions for those that we brought in, probably lasted for a good six weeks before we transitioned to more operational sorts of activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was the fusion centre? Was that something that you set up or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker asked that I help establish the fusion centre. It's a very good point. It was the kind of, I guess, the heartbeat of the organisation. It's where all of our reporting would go into. It's where reports would be written and compiled and disseminated to the OSCE in Vienna. It represented Russians, Americans, Norwegians, various countries. Not all were represented in there. It was sort of an intelligence cell - for a lack of a better word - to pull together information and data and get it disseminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us who of the Russians was a member of the fusion cell or who was there?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't recall any of the names of any of the personnel that worked in the fusion centre. I know that there were no restrictions on the countries that were to be represented in there and participating. As I mentioned, I knew of the Russians, I knew of the American, I knew of the British, I knew of the Norwegians. And that rotated out periodically. People would come four to six months and rotate back and then others would be brought in. So it was the director of the fusion centre, I believe, early on was an American. He left after a short time and a another American came in behind him. I think the deputy in there was a Russian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll get back to the Russian representative a little later, because it seems to me from your notes that there were different positions on whether there should be any Russians at the fusion centre or not because of the information that was shared with NATO, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I do. That was a large issue. There was imagery that we were concerned about sharing in there. Ambassador Walker was concerned about a Russian contingent in there. There were secure phones in there that were US in nature. We found ways to work around those problems to accommodate the Russians. It was important, and Ambassador Walker knew it was important, to have the Russians represented in there. Again, I'm not sure of all of their levels of responsibility or actual capacities and whether they were just reporters or they had true positions of responsibility, but they were a part of the process in the fusion centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What I would like to know is what profile, what kind of experts actually worked at the fusion centre? And I don't mean the personnel at large, I mean the people who did the core functions, who performed the core functions at the fusion centre?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't speak to all the members in the fusion centre. I do know that some of them had intelligence backgrounds. Some of them had collection -- intelligence collection backgrounds. Some of them had Special Forces background. In general, that's what I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who carried out the selection of that cadre?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: From what I can remember the Secretariat put out the advertisements for the positions, and they would, you know, people that were interested would fill out an application and the Secretariat would select the fusion centre. Sometimes we would get mission members on board and recognise their writing skills or their communication skills and sometimes we would take them from the mission, from say from the political office, human rights office, and ask them to come to the fusion centre to work because they wrote well and they could articulate and interpret well. But for the most part, I believe it was the Secretariat, Mr. Krasnai [phoen], I think, down there had a role on selecting how the fusion centre and other fields would be populated. We generally put out what our needs were back to the Secretariat and they would go out and recruit what we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were not the person who ultimately decided on who it was to become a member of the fusion cell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You and Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A thing just came to my mind. Ms. Donna Phelan, did you know her?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't remember that name, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Then I may be wrong. In January 1999, who was appointed as the head of fusion cell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I believe at the time it was a civilian who was an American. I can't be sure, but I believe it was an American.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm certain that up to that time that person was an American by the name of Andy Isruk [phoen]. Do you recall that name?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Army -- army background, I do remember him, yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And I just recalled that it was actually Ms. Donna Phelan who replaced him. At the beginning of your mission, she was or she had been tasked with operations. Another interesting thing is this: I wanted to ask you about the method of total or complete confrontation. Have you ever heard of such a thing?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you don't seem to recall Ms. Donna Phelan?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I sure don't. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well, many years have gone by and many people were involved, Colonel. If I'm correct, perhaps you can correct me if I'm not, but I believe the fusion cell contained two parts; one part was supposed to with summarising the most important events of the day from the reports they received and to provide a collective report to Mr. Walker and his deputies. Am I correct in saying that that was one part of the fusion cell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Or better yet, you tell us what the segments of that work were, because I may go astray and risk you misunderstanding me. So one job to do was to collate a report for a day, have it in one place, and what were the other activities of the fusion cell?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: It was to -- dissemination to the OSCE in Vienna, what was happening in the field. They wanted reports and the fusion centre was providing that because the member states were asking for it. So we had an internal and an external requirement for the fusion centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did it also do something related to security assessment, say, what is going to happen?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall security assessments. You know, from what I can remember, there -- on the reports there was an assessment. I don't know if it was called security assessment, but it was based on the day's events. There were assessments made and analysis done on what we could expect for the next day or the week and sometimes the idea was was to trigger us to bring those things up in meetings as Mr. Sainovic when we were concerned about them. I guess the best way to say is that they conducted some trend analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to yourself, who was in the immediate circle in Mr. Walker's cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Well, each of his deputy heads of mission, which would have been a German and a French, a British, Norwegian, I believe there were five. Then of course his inner office was myself, Albanian and Serb interpreter, and an American secretary from the State Department, and that was generally who was in his staff meetings. Fusion centre director early on attended those staff meetings, which helps me define the inner circle, but that didn't sustain itself for very long. And I'm referring -- I'm referring only to the fusion centre director. The staff meetings were regular occurrences for Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of decision-making mechanism existed in the KVM headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Mr. Walker really made the final decisions. His -- he would take the inputs from each of his deputy heads of mission. There were, you know, inputs from each member regarding everything from a press statement to where humanitarian needs were needed, to where KVM operations needed to be focused, to how we handle missing Serbs and missing Albanians. Discussion and strategy was laid out. He was given advice and then Mr. Walker would make a decision based on that input.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to focus on the most important thing, which is verification as the most important role of the mission. When a meeting takes place and Mr. Walker decides that there was a violation of the agreement, what was the procedure after that? In simple terms. So everything is concluded, it is determined that a certain event amounts to a violation. What follows? What is the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: From what I can remember, it was documented, it was forwarded to the OSCE Mission in Vienna, and we also advised Mr. Sainovic of the violations, of non-compliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who was supposed to implement or put his decision in practice, if anyone? Was it you perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: On occasion I would be asked to make a phone call, but we had a mechanism where the reports were disseminated out of the OSCE KVM to Vienna automatically on a daily basis. On occasion, I would be asked to call Ambassador Travik who was the assistant to Ambassador Vollebaek, CEO. I worked more with him than I did in the early going Mr. Geremek, I believe was his name, in Poland, primarily because we -- when he stood down the mission became operational. So he would inform the chairman of office directly and I often did that through his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, save for such verbal reports, when there was a violation, was there an office that would draft a protest and forward it to the OSCE, or did you forward such a protest letter to anyone in particular? Are you familiar with any of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Our political office, I think, sometimes got involved in that. I don't recall ever writing such reports and sending them off in a unilateral fashion. That was what the staff was to do. I don't recall all of the activities at the political office, but it seems to me they had a role in wording that properly to send it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If such a document existed, was Mr. Walker supposed to sign it?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall if he ever had to sign those or not, sir. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you testified in the Milutinovic case, do you recall being shown a document of that nature? It was an official letter of protest signed by Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I do remember him with letters of protest. I don't remember that specific document, but I do remember letters of protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: And they were [Overlapping speakers] ... presented to Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the problem is that we have to put questions to witnesses and this concerns material --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: This concerns witness's opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: -- if we had all the documents, things would be pretty clear. But if a decision was made that there was non-compliance and we don't have a letter that would show that such protest letters were indeed sent, for example, there was an event that was protested and a letter was sent to Mr. Milosevic, but we don't actually have a letter of protest that I could show you. Are you familiar with any such instances in which occurrences of this nature happened?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Familiar with letters going to Mr. Milosevic? Or just letters of protest?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Letters of protest?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I remember some documents that Mr. Walker wanted on the record that clearly defined non-compliance issues. One of those was in the form of a letter that went in December, verbally, primarily to Mr. Milosevic. We often took them to the government building and spoke to Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lukic and Mr. Loncar. They were also incorporated into some of the KVM reporting where there was non-compliance as interpreted by the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's simplify things. There was a thing on the border on the 25th of February concerning some KVM vehicles, when they were crossing from Macedonia into the FRY. On that occasion, the minister of foreign affairs of the FRY sent a letter of protest to the KVM headquarters in Pristina. It was sent by Mr. Jovanovic. Are there any such letters issued by the KVM headquarters that would resemble situations such as this one that would be sent to the other party, and if so, do you know where we could find that.

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Sir, I cannot answer that easily. I'm not a hundred per cent certain of a formal stand-alone letter of protest that might have been presented by Ambassador Walker. I know that it was documented, and I know that it was in reporting, and I know that it was in a letter to Mr. Milosevic on occasion, but as far as stand-alone letters of protest, I'm just not a hundred per cent certain to be able to tell you that there in fact was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: While we are on the topic of reports, KVM reports, do you recall any problems that the Yugoslav authorities asked that the reports you sent to Vienna and to Mr. Vollebaek as the presiding of the OSCE should be sent to the Yugoslav authorities as well?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I think there was some discussion on that in the government building with Mr. Sainovic. I don't remember what the disposition was as a result of that discussion. I honestly don't know if we did agree to send those to the FRY or not. I suspect not though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Staying with the issue of reports, were there differences in the level of protection or coding of certain documents, were some documents unprotected and some others could only be copied to certain addressees, and I mean the KVM headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Are you referring was there NATO restricted documents that were not authorised for all member states to see versus unrestricted documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a difference in the degree of confidentiality or restriction, and if so, what were the levels and to whom did they apply?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: We -- we did request a desire to be able to handle NATO classified documents. NATO had lots of trouble with that. Putting it in the international mission like that. So what instead was arrived at was a secure phone capability that was in a sound-proof booth that was put in the fusion centre and it was a secure line that -- that the Americans could access and use and NATO member countries could use. I don't think that we ever received the clearance to publish and classify specific documents with NATO classifications. But we did have a secure phone to be able it to discuss issues of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained that in relation to NATO and how it was used. What about the other users, say, the member states and the presiding officer of the OSCE as well as its Secretariat, or perhaps within the mission itself, were there any restrictions in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall any specific restrictions on documents that you are referring to. I think Ambassador Walker had, you know, I guess I would refer to him as eyes-only documents that were met for just his senior staff that weren't meant for the review of the KVM mission at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that you were Mr. Walker's closest associate, do you recall whether there were any problems in the drafting of reports sent to the OSCE Secretariat in Vienna, that is to say, that the reports of certain verifiers were not being forwarded to Vienna, but rather kept in Pristina only?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any reports that were purposely held back by Ambassador Walker not to go to Vienna. I'm unaware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If my memory is correct, on the 12th of February, 1999, you were with Mr. Walker during his visit to Moscow; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether the Russian side had any objections to make as to the reports of their verifiers and their reports being sent to the headquarters in Pristina complaining about those reports not being sent to Vienna, it was actually sent to the Vienna Secretariat directly by the Russian side as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I don't recall that kind of thing or discussion on that. And if you're looking for was there disagreements in the mission about various events intent of an operation, results of an operation, there was discussion with Ambassador Walker and his staff, there were contentious arguments with the French ambassador, Ambassador Keller and Ambassador Walker on interpretation. So there were certainly issues. Ambassador Walker did have the final say on contentious issues and how it would be worded and how it would go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I was confused when I learned that, in addition to the verifiers sending their reports to the headquarter, they also sent reports to their respective states. Was this also a practice in the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, this was occurring on a frequent basis and concerned Mr. Walker greatly. He was not happy that there were member states that work international mission were sending things home to their member states, to their home office, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, could you tell us which were the basic documents you applied in the process of verification?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I can't recall the documents. I know one of the documents of course was the agreement. I believe there were others, but I don't recall their name or their title. It's just been too long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. When I say "you," I don't mean you personally but the verification mission, you should know that. Would you agree with me that the basis of the verification process was laid down by Resolution 1199 by the Security Council of the UN?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Exhibit D160 on the screen. Can we see page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the third paragraph from the top, am I right in saying that violence exerted by any of the sides, as well as terrorism committed by individuals or groups in order to achieve political goals is condemned as is any such activity in Kosovo coming from outside of the country, including the supply of arms and training for terrorist activities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: And the question, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is this: In view of this paragraph in the preamble to the resolution, what actions did the mission take in order to prevent, to stop, the supply of arms and training for terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MICHAEL PHILLIPS
utterances.text: I know that it was a deep concern to Ambassador Walker. He wanted assets and money frozen so they couldn't procure weapons. We did not want the KLA to have new weapons or more weapons. It was a concern that was delivered to us from Mr. Sainovic. And it was a concern that we agreed with and that we delivered to the OSCE Mission in Vienna. I think we also raised this issue with Ambassador Holbrooke that it needed to stop, it wasn't helping us.
